newsitem.title: SPAIN: FORECAST - Iberian bonds ready to rally next week.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Iberian bonds ready to rally next week.

text.p: Spanish and Portuguese assets are expected to rally next week on revived euro-optimism following a week of jitters over France's reluctance to accept the budget stability pact at next week's EU summit.
"Sentiment is turning very positive toward peripherals," said Graham McDevitt, head of bond strategy at Paribas in London.
"In the past weeks we have seen foreign selling, but domestic buying supported these markets. Now that France and Germany seem to have sorted things out, we expect two to three weeks of rally."

By refocusing on France's priority for jobs, EU leaders seem to have managed to secure Paris' prompt agreement to the stability pact. Markets will closely watch the summit in Amsterdam on Monday and Tuesday, assuming that leaders will approve the fiscal discipline measures.
Another event likely to make France's position on EMU clearer will be the June 19 speech of new leftwing French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin.
Following the announcement of benign Spanish May CPI, the Spanish 10-year spread over Bunds was trading little changed at around 73 basis points. It hit a record low on May 21 at 64 basis points.
"(Next week) we could reach a new low at around 60 basis points," said Valentin Fernandez at Credit Lyonnais in Madrid.
A test of 60 to 65 basis points in the next one to two weeks would not be unexpected, said David Brown, chief European economist at Bear Stearns in London.

On Thursday -- as Lisbon was closed on Friday for a local bank holiday -- the Portuguese spread was trading at around 73 basis points, lower than a week ago, but for the first time higher than its Spanish counterpart.
"If we have a large euro membership, there's no reason why Portugal should trade better than Spain," Fernandez said.
As a weak euro becomes more likely, the previous rule of thumb that saw Portugal favoured over Spain and Spain favoured over Italy ceased to run true, analysts said.
As a result, Italy may outpace Iberia in a general improvement in peripherals next week.
"We suggested our clients shift money in the short end from Spain into Italy, as the Bank of Italy has more room left to cut its official rate than Spain," said Fernandez.
Although Spanish inflation hit an almost 30-year low in May, many analysts expect the Bank of Spain to keep its official money market rate unchanged at 5.25 percent.

A Reuter poll conducted on Friday after the release of CPI showed that 12 out of 13 analysts were ruling out a rate cut on Monday, although seven of them were expecting a new monetary easing -- the fifth rate cut this year -- by the end of June.
Within Iberia, Portugal offers a better outlook at the short end of the yield curve than Spain, analysts said.

Portuguese May CPI, out on Tuesday, is expected to show a fall to 1.5 percent down from 1.8 percent in April and analysts stressed that the Bank of Portugal has more scope for declines than its Spanish equivalent.
"We expect the Bank of Portugal to cut both absorption and repo rate by about 25 to 30 basis points," said Martin Amaru Neto at Banco Essi in Lisbon on Thursday.
Now the two official rates stand at 6.0 and 5.75 percent respectively "although it's likely the central bank will wait until the Amsterdam summit is over".
-- Madrid Newsroom, + 341 585 8340
